name: Programming Fundamentals

beginner.content:
What is a Variable?

A variable is a named location in memory that holds a value your program can use and change while it runs.

Think of it like a labeled box: the label (variable name) never changes, but you can swap out what's inside the box (the value) as your program executes.

In Java, every variable must have a type declared before it can be used - this tells the compiler what kind of data (and how much memory) the box can hold.

Declaring vs Initializing

Declaration tells the compiler "this name exists and this is its type." Initialization gives it a starting value. You can do both together, or declare now and initialize later.

Naming Rules for Variables

• Must start with a letter, underscore (_), or dollar sign ($) - never a digit.
• Can contain letters, digits, underscores, and dollar signs after the first character.
• Case-sensitive: age and Age are different variables.
• By convention, Java variable names use camelCase (e.g. studentName, totalMarks).
• Cannot use reserved keywords like int, class, public as variable names.

Variables Can Change - That's the Point

The word "variable" literally means "able to vary." Unlike a constant, a variable's stored value can be reassigned any number of times during program execution, which is what allows programs to react to input, loop, and compute.

expert.content:
Categories of Variables in Java

Java has three kinds of variables, distinguished by where they are declared and how long they live:

TypeDeclared WhereLifetimeDefault Value?
Local variableInside a method/blockOnly while the method/block executesNo - must be initialized before use
Instance variableInside class, outside any methodAs long as the object existsYes - gets a default (0, null, false, etc.)
Static (class) variableInside class, marked staticEntire program run, shared by all objectsYes - gets a default

Variables Are Not Values - They Are References to Storage

Conceptually a variable binds a name to a memory slot. For primitives, that slot directly holds the value. For objects, the slot holds a reference (an address) pointing to the object's data on the heap. This distinction explains a lot of confusing behavior for beginners.

int x = 10;              String s = new String("hi");

Stack:                   Stack:            Heap:
+---+                    +-------+         +------+
| x | 10                 |   s   |-------->| "hi" |
+---+                    +-------+         +------+

Scope and Shadowing

A variable's scope is the region of code where it can be referenced. Local variables are scoped to the block { } they are declared in and disappear once that block ends. When an inner scope declares a variable with the same name as an outer one, Java either flags it as a compile error (for local-in-local) or allows "shadowing" (for instance variables hidden by local ones).

final Variables: Write-Once

Marking a variable final makes it assignable exactly once. This is how Java expresses "constant" at the variable level - useful for values that must never change after being set, and required for local variables captured by lambdas/anonymous classes.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the difference between a local and an instance variable?Local variables live inside a method/block and must be initialized before use; instance variables belong to an object, live as long as the object, and get default values automatically
Do local variables get default values in Java?No - the compiler forces you to initialize them before first use, unlike instance/static variables
What happens when you assign one object reference variable to another?Both variables end up pointing to the same object on the heap - changes through either reference are visible via both
What is variable shadowing?When a variable in an inner scope has the same name as one in an outer scope, hiding the outer one within that inner scope
What does the final keyword do to a variable?Makes it assignable only once - any later reassignment is a compile-time error
Can a static variable be accessed without creating an object?Yes - it belongs to the class itself, so it can be accessed via ClassName.variableName
Why must a lambda only capture effectively final local variables?Because the lambda may outlive the method's stack frame, so Java copies the value at capture time and forbids further reassignment to keep that copy consistent

beginner.content:
What is Data?

Data is any piece of information a program works with - numbers, text, true/false answers, dates, images, and so on. A program's job, at its core, is to take some data in, transform it, and produce new data out.

In Java, every piece of data has a type, which tells the compiler what kind of values are allowed and what operations make sense on it.

Primitive Data Types

Java has 8 built-in "primitive" types for the most basic kinds of data - whole numbers, decimals, single characters, and booleans. They hold raw values directly, not references.

Reference (Object) Data

Beyond primitives, data can also be an object - a bundle of related values and behavior, like a String (text), an array (a list of values), or a custom class (e.g. Student). These are called "reference types" because the variable holds a pointer to the data, not the data itself.

Why Data Types Matter

The type of data determines how much memory it needs and what operations are valid. You can add two numbers, but adding a number and a boolean directly makes no sense - the compiler catches this kind of mistake for you before the program ever runs.

expert.content:
Primitive vs Reference Data - Where It Lives

This distinction drives almost everything about how Java manages memory and passes data around.

AspectPrimitive DataReference (Object) Data
Examplesint, double, char, boolean, long, float, byte, shortString, arrays, custom classes, wrapper classes
StorageActual value stored directly in the variable's slotVariable holds a reference (address); actual data lives on the heap
Default value (as field)0 / 0.0 / false / '\u0000'null
Copy behaviorAssignment copies the valueAssignment copies the reference (both point to same object)

The 8 Primitive Types - Size and Range

TypeSizeTypical Use
byte1 byteSmall integers, memory-tight arrays
short2 bytesRarely used, legacy interop
int4 bytesDefault choice for whole numbers
long8 bytesVery large whole numbers (timestamps, IDs)
float4 bytesDecimal numbers, low precision needs
double8 bytesDefault choice for decimal numbers
char2 bytesA single Unicode character
booleanJVM-dependent (conceptually 1 bit)true/false flags

Wrapper Classes: Bridging Primitives and Objects

Since primitives are not objects, Java provides a wrapper class for each one (int -> Integer, double -> Double, etc.) so primitive data can be used where objects are required - like in collections (List<Integer>). Autoboxing and unboxing convert between the two automatically.

Type Conversion: Widening vs Narrowing

Data of one type can often be converted to another. Widening (small type -> big type) happens automatically because no data is lost. Narrowing (big type -> small type) requires an explicit cast because precision or range can be lost.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the difference between primitive and reference data types?Primitives store the actual value directly; references store the address of an object living on the heap
Why does Java need wrapper classes?To let primitive values be treated as objects, e.g. for use in generic collections like List<Integer>
What is autoboxing?The compiler's automatic conversion of a primitive value into its corresponding wrapper object
Why is a narrowing conversion required to be explicit?Because it can lose data (precision or range), so the compiler forces the programmer to acknowledge the risk with a cast
What is the default value of an uninitialized boolean instance field?false
Is String a primitive type in Java?No - String is a reference type (a class), even though it behaves like a value type in many ways
What happens if you assign a double literal to an int variable directly?Compile error - it's a narrowing conversion and requires an explicit cast

beginner.content:
Why Programs Need Memory

Every variable, object, and piece of running code needs somewhere to "live" while the program executes - that place is the computer's memory (RAM). When you run a Java program, the JVM (Java Virtual Machine) sets aside memory regions to store method calls and the objects your program creates.

Two Main Areas: Stack and Heap

Java divides memory into two important areas for running code: the stack (for method calls and local variables) and the heap (for objects created with new). Understanding which area something lives in helps explain how Java programs behave.

Memory is Freed Automatically (Garbage Collection)

Unlike some languages where you must manually free memory, Java's Garbage Collector (GC) automatically finds objects that are no longer reachable by any variable and reclaims their memory, preventing manual memory-management bugs.

Running Out of Memory

Memory is not infinite. If a program keeps creating objects that never become unreachable, or if a method calls itself endlessly, the JVM eventually runs out of memory and throws an error.

expert.content:
Stack vs Heap - The Core Model

STACK (per thread)                    HEAP (shared, one per JVM)
+----------------------+              +----------------------------+
| main() frame         |              |                            |
|  int x = 5           |              |  new Person("Raoji", 22)   |
|  Person p ---------------------->   |  { name: "Raoji",          |
|                       |              |    age: 22 }               |
+----------------------+              |                            |
| greet() frame         |              +----------------------------+
|  (pushed on call,     |
|   popped on return)   |
+----------------------+
The stack holds method call frames (local variables, parameters, return addresses) and is LIFO (last-in-first-out) - frames are pushed on call and popped on return. The heap holds all objects created with new, and persists until garbage collected.

AspectStackHeap
StoresMethod frames, local variables, primitives, referencesAll objects and arrays (the actual data)
LifetimeTied to the method call - freed when method returnsTied to reachability - freed by GC when unreachable
Allocation speedVery fast (just move a pointer)Slower (bookkeeping required)
Thread sharingEach thread has its own stackShared across all threads
Failure modeStackOverflowError (too much nesting/recursion)OutOfMemoryError (too many live objects)

Method Call Stack in Action

Each method call pushes a new frame onto the stack; returning pops it off. This is why recursion consumes stack memory proportional to recursion depth.

Garbage Collection: Reachability, Not Reference Counting

The GC does not simply count references - it periodically traces from a set of "GC roots" (active thread stacks, static fields) and marks every object reachable from them as live. Anything unreached is garbage, even if it's part of a reference cycle (two objects pointing at each other but reachable from nowhere).

Common Memory Errors

ErrorRegionTypical Cause
StackOverflowErrorStackInfinite or excessively deep recursion (no base case, or base case never reached)
OutOfMemoryError: Java heap spaceHeapToo many live objects retained (e.g. growing a list forever, memory leak via static collections)

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the difference between stack and heap memory?Stack stores method frames/local variables and is freed automatically on return; heap stores objects and is freed by the garbage collector when unreachable
What causes a StackOverflowError?Excessively deep or infinite recursion that keeps pushing frames onto the stack until it's exhausted
What causes an OutOfMemoryError?The heap fills with live (still-reachable) objects faster than the GC can reclaim space, e.g. a memory leak
Does the garbage collector use reference counting?No - the standard JVM GC uses reachability analysis from GC roots, which correctly collects reference cycles too
Is each thread's stack shared with other threads?No - every thread gets its own private stack; the heap is shared across all threads
Can you force garbage collection to run immediately?You can request it with System.gc(), but it is only a hint - the JVM decides if/when to actually run it
Where do static variables live?In the method area (part of the JVM's memory, sometimes called metaspace), not the stack or per-object heap space

beginner.content:
What is an Algorithm?

An algorithm is a precise, step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem or completing a task - like a recipe for a computer. Every program you write, no matter how simple, follows some algorithm.

A good algorithm is:
• Well-defined - each step is unambiguous.
• Finite - it eventually terminates.
• Effective - each step can actually be carried out.

From Plain English to Code

Before writing code, it helps to describe the algorithm in plain steps (pseudocode). For example, "to check if a number is even: divide it by 2, if the remainder is 0 it's even, otherwise it's odd." Only after the logic is clear do we translate it into Java.

Searching: A Classic Algorithm

Searching means finding whether a value exists in a collection, and where. The simplest approach - linear search - checks every item one by one until a match is found or the list ends.

Sorting: Another Classic Algorithm

Sorting arranges data into a defined order (ascending/descending). A simple example is bubble sort, which repeatedly compares neighboring elements and swaps them if they're out of order.

expert.content:
Why Algorithms Matter: Efficiency

Two algorithms can solve the exact same problem and produce the exact same output, yet take wildly different amounts of time or memory. We measure this with time complexity, usually expressed in Big-O notation - a description of how the runtime grows as input size (n) grows.

Big-ONameExample
O(1)ConstantAccessing an array element by index
O(log n)LogarithmicBinary search on a sorted array
O(n)LinearLinear search, single loop over n items
O(n log n)LinearithmicEfficient sorts (merge sort, quicksort average case)
O(n^2)QuadraticBubble sort, nested loops over the same data

Linear Search vs Binary Search

Binary search is dramatically faster than linear search, but it has a prerequisite: the data must already be sorted. It repeatedly halves the search space by comparing the target to the middle element.

Algorithm Design Strategies

Most algorithms fall into a handful of general design patterns:

StrategyIdeaExample
Brute forceTry every possibilityChecking all pairs for a matching sum
Divide and conquerSplit problem into smaller subproblems, solve, combineMerge sort, binary search
GreedyMake the locally best choice at each stepCoin change with standard denominations
Dynamic programmingBreak into overlapping subproblems, cache resultsFibonacci with memoization

Space Complexity: The Other Half of Efficiency

Time isn't the only cost - algorithms also use extra memory (space complexity). A recursive solution might be simple to read but use O(n) stack space, while an iterative version of the same logic might use only O(1) extra space.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What makes something an "algorithm" vs just "code"?An algorithm is the language-independent logical procedure; code is one specific implementation of that procedure in a language
What is Big-O notation used for?Describing how an algorithm's running time (or space) grows as the input size grows, ignoring constant factors
Why is binary search faster than linear search?It eliminates half the remaining search space each step (O(log n)) instead of checking one element at a time (O(n)) - but it requires sorted data
What is the time complexity of bubble sort in the worst case?O(n^2), because of the nested comparison loops
What is the difference between time complexity and space complexity?Time complexity measures how runtime scales with input size; space complexity measures how extra memory usage scales with input size
What is memoization?Caching results of expensive function calls so repeated calls with the same input return instantly instead of recomputing
Give an example of a greedy algorithm.Making change with the fewest coins by always picking the largest denomination that fits, when denominations allow it

beginner.content:
What is a Flowchart?

A flowchart is a diagram that shows the step-by-step flow of an algorithm using standard shapes connected by arrows. Before writing code, drawing a flowchart helps you visualize the logic and catch mistakes early.

Common shapes:
• Oval - Start / End
• Rectangle - Process / action step
• Diamond - Decision (yes/no branch)
• Parallelogram - Input / Output
• Arrow - Flow of control from one step to the next

A Simple Flowchart: Check Even or Odd

      ( Start )
          |
   [ Read number n ]
          |
     < n % 2 == 0? >
       /        \
    Yes          No
     |            |
[ Print "Even" ] [ Print "Odd" ]
     \            /
      \          /
        ( End )
This maps directly onto Java code with an if-else statement.

Flowcharting a Loop

A loop in a flowchart is drawn as an arrow that goes back to an earlier decision point, forming a cycle that repeats until a condition becomes false.
   ( Start )
      |
 [ i = 1 ]
      |<------------+
 < i <= 5? >         |
   / \               |
 Yes  No              |
  |    |               |
[Print i] ( End )      |
  |                    |
[ i = i + 1 ]----------+

Why Flowcharts Help Beginners

Flowcharts force you to think through every branch and every repeat before typing a single line of code. They are especially useful for spotting missing cases - for example, forgetting what happens when a loop condition is never true.

expert.content:
Standard Flowchart Symbols (ANSI/ISO)

ShapeMeaningJava Equivalent
Oval / TerminatorStart or End of the programBeginning/end of main()
Rectangle / ProcessAn action or computationAn assignment statement or method call
Diamond / DecisionA yes/no or true/false branchif / else / switch
Parallelogram / I-OReading input or printing outputScanner.nextInt(), System.out.println()
Circle / ConnectorLinks flowchart parts across a pageN/A - a documentation aid only
ArrowDirection of control flowSequential execution / jump on branch or loop

Flowchart of a Nested Decision (Grading System)

        ( Start )
            |
     [ Read marks ]
            |
      < marks >= 90? >-- Yes --> [ Print "A" ] --+
            | No                                  |
      < marks >= 75? >-- Yes --> [ Print "B" ] --+
            | No                                  |
      < marks >= 50? >-- Yes --> [ Print "C" ] --+
            | No                                  |
      [ Print "F" ] --------------------------------+
                                                    |
                                                ( End )
This chain of diamonds is a direct visual model of an if / else-if / else-if / else ladder.

Flowchart to Pseudocode to Code: The Translation Pipeline

Flowchart ElementPseudocodeJava
Diamond with two exitsIF condition THEN ... ELSE ...if (condition) { ... } else { ... }
Loop-back arrow to a decisionWHILE condition DO ... END WHILEwhile (condition) { ... }
Sequence of rectanglesStep 1; Step 2; Step 3stmt1; stmt2; stmt3;
Parallelogram (input)READ nint n = scanner.nextInt();
This pipeline - flowchart to pseudocode to code - is exactly how algorithms taught conceptually get turned into real, compilable Java.

When Flowcharts Break Down

Flowcharts are great for small, linear algorithms, but they scale poorly for large real-world systems: they become unreadable spaghetti diagrams for deeply nested logic, and they don't capture concepts like object relationships, concurrency, or exceptions well. For those, professionals use other notations - UML class/sequence diagrams, pseudocode, or just well-structured code with comments.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What shape represents a decision in a flowchart?A diamond, with typically two outgoing arrows labeled Yes/No or True/False
How is a loop represented in a flowchart?An arrow that loops back from a later step to an earlier decision point, repeating until the condition is false
What is the difference between a flowchart and pseudocode?A flowchart is a visual/graphical representation of logic; pseudocode is a text-based, language-agnostic description of the same logic
Why draw a flowchart before coding?It helps clarify logic, catch missing branches/edge cases, and communicate an algorithm to others before implementation
What symbol denotes Start/End in a flowchart?An oval (terminator symbol)
When do flowcharts become impractical?For large, deeply nested, or highly concurrent logic - they become unreadable and other notations (UML, structured code) communicate better

beginner.content:
What is a Condition?

A condition is an expression that evaluates to either true or false. Programs use conditions to make decisions - to run one block of code instead of another depending on the current state of the data.

The if Statement

The if statement runs a block of code only when its condition is true. If the condition is false, the block is simply skipped.

if-else: Two Paths

Adding else gives your program a second path to take when the condition is false, so exactly one of the two blocks always runs.

Multiple Conditions with else-if

When there are more than two possible outcomes, chain conditions with else if. Java checks them top to bottom and runs the first one that is true.

Combining Conditions: && and ||

Simple conditions can be combined into compound ones: && (AND) requires both sides to be true; || (OR) requires at least one side to be true.

expert.content:
How Java Evaluates Conditions: Short-Circuiting

Java's logical operators && and || are short-circuiting: they stop evaluating as soon as the result is already determined. This isn't just an optimization - it's often relied upon to avoid errors, like checking an object isn't null before dereferencing it.

OperatorStops Early WhenNon-short-circuit Equivalent
&&Left side is false (result must be false)& (evaluates both sides always)
||Left side is true (result must be true)| (evaluates both sides always)

The switch Statement: A Structured Alternative to else-if Chains

When checking one variable against many discrete values, a long else-if chain gets unwieldy. switch expresses this more clearly, and modern Java's arrow syntax also avoids the classic "fall-through" bug of forgetting break.

The Ternary Operator: A Condition as an Expression

The ternary operator condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse lets you use a condition to directly produce a value, instead of writing a full if-else block just to assign a variable.

Common Condition Pitfalls

PitfallWhy It's a Problem
Using = instead of == = is assignment, == is comparison; Java's boolean-only if condition thankfully catches this at compile time for non-boolean types
Comparing objects (e.g. String) with ==== compares references, not content; use .equals() to compare values
Forgetting break in a classic switchExecution "falls through" into the next case unintentionally
Deeply nested if-else chainsHard to read/maintain - often better refactored into switch, early returns, or separate methods

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is short-circuit evaluation?&& and || stop evaluating as soon as the overall result is already determined, skipping the right-hand operand when possible
What is the difference between & and && in a condition?& always evaluates both operands; && short-circuits and skips the right side when the left already determines the result
Why should you use .equals() instead of == for Strings?== compares object references (memory addresses); .equals() compares actual character content
What happens if you omit break in a classic switch statement?Execution falls through and continues into the next case's code until a break or the end of the switch
Can a switch statement's condition be a String in Java?Yes, since Java 7 switch supports String, along with int/char/enum and their wrapper types
What type must an if condition evaluate to in Java?boolean - unlike some languages, Java does not allow ints or other types to be used directly as truthy/falsy conditions
When is a ternary expression preferred over if-else?When the sole purpose of the branch is to compute/assign a single value - it's more concise for simple cases

beginner.content:
What is Looping?

Looping means repeating a block of code multiple times, instead of writing the same statement over and over by hand. It exists because many real problems require doing the same action for every item in a collection, or repeating a step until some condition is met.

Without loops, printing "Hello" 5 times would need 5 separate print statements. With a loop, one statement does it.

Counting Loops

The most common kind of loop repeats a known, fixed number of times - counting up from a start value to an end value. Java's for loop is built specifically for this pattern.

Condition-Based Loops

Sometimes you don't know in advance how many times to repeat - you just repeat "while some condition holds." Java's while loop handles this: it checks the condition before every repetition.

Looping Over a Collection

A very common looping style is "for each item in this collection, do something with it" - without needing to manage a counter manually. Java's enhanced for loop (for-each) expresses exactly this idea.

expert.content:
Why Looping is a Fundamental Concept, Not Just Syntax

Looping is one of the three foundational control-flow building blocks of programming (alongside sequence and selection/branching). Any repeatable computation - processing every row in a database, retrying a network call, animating a frame every 16ms - is, at its heart, a loop. Different languages express it differently, but the underlying idea is the same: "repeat this action, either a known number of times, or until a condition changes."

Looping StyleWhen You KnowJava Construct
Count-controlledExact number of repetitions in advancefor
Condition-controlled (pre-test)A condition to check before each repetitionwhile
Condition-controlled (post-test)Must run at least once, then check a conditiondo-while
Collection-controlledIterating every element of a groupfor-each (enhanced for)

Two Looping Styles Compared: Recursion vs Iteration

Repetition doesn't require a loop keyword at all - recursion (a function calling itself) achieves the same repeated-work effect using the call stack instead of a loop construct. Both compute the same result; they differ in mechanism and cost.

The Anatomy of a Loop: Init, Condition, Update, Body

Every counting loop, regardless of language or syntax, has four logical parts. Recognizing them helps you translate between loop styles and spot infinite-loop bugs.

for ( INIT ; CONDITION ; UPDATE ) {
        BODY
}

INIT      -> runs once, before the loop starts   (int i = 0)
CONDITION -> checked before every repetition      (i < 5)
BODY      -> the code that actually repeats       (System.out.println(i))
UPDATE    -> runs after each repetition            (i++)
If UPDATE never makes CONDITION false, you get an infinite loop - one of the most common beginner bugs.

Nested Loops and Early Exit

Loops can contain other loops (nested loops), useful for processing 2D data like grids or tables. break exits a loop early; continue skips to the next iteration without exiting.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is looping, conceptually?Repeating a block of logic multiple times, either a known number of times or until a condition changes, instead of duplicating code manually
What's the difference between a pre-test and post-test loop?A pre-test loop (while) checks its condition before running the body - it may run zero times; a post-test loop (do-while) runs the body first, then checks - it always runs at least once
Can any counting loop be rewritten as recursion, and vice versa?Yes - both are ways to express repetition; loops use a control construct with constant memory, recursion uses self-calls and stack memory
What are the four logical parts of a for loop?Initialization, condition, body, and update
What causes an infinite loop?A condition that never becomes false, usually because the update step is missing or doesn't move the loop variable toward the exit condition
What is the difference between break and continue?break exits the loop entirely; continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one

beginner.content:
What is a Function?

A function (called a "method" in Java when it belongs to a class) is a named, reusable block of code that performs a specific task. Instead of copy-pasting the same logic everywhere it's needed, you define it once and "call" it by name wherever it's needed.

Parameters: Feeding Data In

Functions become far more useful when they can accept input. Parameters are placeholders in the function definition; when you call the function, you supply actual values (arguments) for them.

Return Values: Getting Data Out

A function can send a result back to whoever called it, using return. The function's declared return type tells you what kind of value to expect.

Why Break Code into Functions?

Functions make programs easier to read, test, and fix, because each one handles one clear job. This idea is called modularity - build the program from small, well-named, independent pieces rather than one giant block of code.

expert.content:
Java Passes Everything by Value

A common point of confusion: Java is always pass-by-value - there is no pass-by-reference. What varies is what the value is: for primitives, the value is the actual data (a copy is passed, so the caller's variable is untouched). For objects, the value is a copy of the reference (the address) - so the method can modify the object's internal state through that reference, but reassigning the parameter itself never affects the caller's variable.

The Call Stack: Where Function Calls Live

Every function call gets its own stack frame holding its parameters, local variables, and the address to return to. Calling a function pushes a frame; returning pops it. This is why each call to a function is independent, even recursive calls to itself.

main() calls square(5)

Stack (grows downward):
+---------------------+
| main() frame         |
|   result = ?          |
+---------------------+
| square(5) frame       |   <- pushed on call
|   number = 5           |
+---------------------+   <- popped on return, result flows back to main

Overloading: Same Name, Different Signatures

Java allows multiple functions (methods) to share a name as long as their parameter lists differ in type, number, or order - this is called overloading. The compiler picks the correct one to call based on the arguments provided, at compile time.

Pure vs Impure Functions

AspectPure FunctionImpure Function
Output depends onOnly its input parametersInput parameters AND/OR external/mutable state
Side effectsNone - doesn't modify anything outside itselfMay print, modify fields, write files, etc.
Same input -> same output?AlwaysNot guaranteed
Easy to test?Very easy - fully predictableHarder - depends on external state

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?Always pass-by-value - for objects, the "value" being passed is a copy of the reference, not the object itself
If you reassign an object parameter inside a method, does the caller see the change?No - only the local copy of the reference is reassigned; the caller's original reference still points to the original object
What is method overloading?Defining multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists (type/number/order), resolved at compile time
What is a pure function?A function whose output depends only on its inputs and produces no observable side effects
What does each function call get on the call stack?Its own independent stack frame holding parameters, local variables, and the return address
Can two overloaded methods differ only by return type?No - return type alone is not enough to distinguish overloads; the compiler needs a difference in the parameter list
What is a side effect in the context of functions?Any observable change a function makes outside its own local scope, such as modifying a field, printing, or writing to a file

beginner.content:
What is Recursion?

Recursion is when a function solves a problem by calling itself with a smaller version of the same problem. Each call works on a slightly simpler input, until the problem becomes so simple it can be answered directly, without any further calls.

Every Recursive Function Needs a Base Case

The base case is the simplest version of the problem - one that can be answered directly, without recursing further. Without a base case, a recursive function would call itself forever (until the program crashes).

The Recursive Case: Reducing Toward the Base Case

The recursive case is where the function calls itself, but with input that is closer to the base case than before. Every recursive call must make progress toward that base case, or the recursion never ends.

A Simple Real Example: Counting Digits

Recursion is a natural fit whenever a problem can be defined in terms of a smaller version of itself. Counting the digits of a number is one such problem: "the digit count of n is 1 plus the digit count of n with its last digit removed."

expert.content:
Visualizing the Call Stack During Recursion

Each recursive call pushes a new stack frame with its own copy of the parameters and local variables. The calls "wind up" (going deeper) until the base case is hit, then "unwind" (returning) as each frame completes and is popped.

factorial(4)
  calls factorial(3)
    calls factorial(2)
      calls factorial(1)
        calls factorial(0) -> returns 1   (base case hit)
      factorial(1) returns 1 * 1  = 1
    factorial(2) returns 2 * 1  = 2
  factorial(3) returns 3 * 2  = 6
factorial(4) returns 4 * 6  = 24

Stack while factorial(0) is executing (deepest point):
+----------------+
| factorial(4)    |  n=4, waiting for factorial(3)
+----------------+
| factorial(3)    |  n=3, waiting for factorial(2)
+----------------+
| factorial(2)    |  n=2, waiting for factorial(1)
+----------------+
| factorial(1)    |  n=1, waiting for factorial(0)
+----------------+
| factorial(0)    |  n=0, returns 1 immediately (base case)
+----------------+

Missing or Wrong Base Case: StackOverflowError

If the base case is missing, unreachable, or the recursive call doesn't actually move toward it, the function keeps calling itself until the stack runs out of space, throwing a StackOverflowError.

Recursion vs Iteration: Cost Trade-off

AspectRecursionIteration (loop)
Extra memoryO(depth) - one stack frame per callO(1) typically - just loop variables
Readability for naturally recursive problemsOften clearer (tree traversal, divide & conquer)Can require an explicit stack/queue to mimic recursion
RiskStackOverflowError on deep/unbounded recursionInfinite loop if the condition never becomes false
Does Java optimize tail calls?No - unlike some languages, the JVM does not perform tail-call eliminationN/A

Why Some Problems Are Naturally Recursive

Certain data structures and problems are themselves defined recursively - a tree is "a node plus two smaller trees," so traversing it recursively mirrors its own definition and is often clearer than the equivalent iterative code with a manual stack.

What are the two essential parts of every recursive function?A base case (stops the recursion) and a recursive case (calls itself with a smaller/simpler input)
What happens if the base case is missing or unreachable?The function keeps calling itself indefinitely, eventually exhausting the stack and throwing StackOverflowError
Does Java optimize tail-recursive calls the way some functional languages do?No - the JVM does not perform tail-call elimination, so even tail-recursive Java code still consumes stack frames per call

Why might recursion be preferred over iteration despite the memory cost?For problems that are naturally recursive in structure (e.g. tree/graph traversal), recursive code mirrors the problem's own definition and is often much easier to read and verify
What determines how much stack memory a recursive call uses?The maximum recursion depth - each nested call adds one more stack frame until the base case is reached and frames start unwinding

beginner.content:
What is Input/Output (I/O)?

Input is data flowing into a program (from the keyboard, a file, a network, etc.), and output is data flowing out of a program (to the screen, a file, a database, etc.). Almost every useful program needs to interact with the outside world this way, rather than working on hard-coded data alone.

Output with System.out

The simplest form of output in Java is printing to the console using System.out.println() (prints with a newline) or System.out.print() (prints without one).

Input with Scanner

To read input typed by the user, Java provides the Scanner class, which reads from System.in (the keyboard, by default).

Reading Different Types of Input

Scanner has different methods for different data types - nextInt() for whole numbers, nextDouble() for decimals, nextLine() for a full line of text, and more.

expert.content:
Streams: The Underlying I/O Model

Java models all I/O as streams - a sequence of data flowing from a source to a destination, one piece at a time. There are two families: byte streams (raw binary data, classes ending in Stream, e.g. FileInputStream) and character streams (text data with encoding handling, classes ending in Reader/Writer, e.g. FileReader).

Stream FamilyHandlesBase ClassesExample
Byte streamsRaw binary data (images, any file)InputStream / OutputStreamFileInputStream, FileOutputStream
Character streamsText, with character-encoding awarenessReader / WriterFileReader, FileWriter, BufferedReader

Buffered I/O: Reducing Costly Round-Trips

Reading or writing one byte/character at a time is slow, because each raw operation may involve a costly system call. Buffered streams (BufferedReader, BufferedWriter, BufferedInputStream) collect data in an in-memory buffer and only perform the underlying I/O operation in larger chunks, dramatically improving performance.

try-with-resources: Guaranteeing Streams Get Closed

Every open stream holds an operating-system resource (a file handle, a socket). Forgetting to close it leaks resources. Java's try-with-resources statement automatically closes any resource implementing AutoCloseable when the block exits - even if an exception is thrown - so you never need a manual finally { close(); }.

Standard I/O Streams: System.in, System.out, System.err

Every Java program is handed three pre-connected streams by the JVM at startup: System.in (standard input, usually the keyboard), System.out (standard output, usually the console), and System.err (standard error, also usually the console, but kept separate so errors can be redirected independently from normal output).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the difference between byte streams and character streams in Java?Byte streams (InputStream/OutputStream) handle raw binary data; character streams (Reader/Writer) handle text and account for character encoding
Why use buffered streams instead of raw streams?They reduce the number of expensive low-level I/O operations by batching reads/writes through an in-memory buffer, improving performance significantly
What problem does try-with-resources solve?It guarantees that any AutoCloseable resource (streams, Scanner, etc.) is closed automatically when the block exits, even on an exception - preventing resource leaks
What are the three standard streams every Java program has access to?System.in (input), System.out (output), System.err (error output)
Why is System.err kept separate from System.out?So error output and normal output can be redirected/logged independently, e.g. in shell scripting
What class is commonly used to read user input from the console in Java?java.util.Scanner, wrapping System.in
What happens if you don't close an open file stream?The underlying OS resource (file handle) stays allocated until the JVM eventually reclaims it (or not at all), which can exhaust available file handles over time

beginner.content:
Linear Search vs Binary Search

  • Linear Search - O(n): checks every element one by one. Works on any array, sorted or not.
  • Binary Search - O(log n): repeatedly halves the search range by comparing the middle element. REQUIRES the array to be sorted first.

Bubble Sort - O(n²)

Repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them if out of order, "bubbling" the largest unsorted element to the end each pass. Simple to understand, but inefficient for large inputs.

intermediate.content:
Merge Sort - O(n log n)

A "divide and conquer" algorithm: recursively splits the array in half until each piece has 1 element, then merges the sorted halves back together. Much faster than O(n²) sorts on large inputs, and stable (equal elements keep their relative order).

beginner.content:
This topic focuses on designing algorithms recursively - taking a real problem and expressing its solution as a smaller version of itself. We assume you already know that a recursive method is one that calls itself; here we practice building recursive solutions step by step.

Every recursive algorithm needs two things:
• A base case - the simplest input, solved directly without further recursion.
• A recursive case - breaks the problem into a smaller version of itself, plus a call to the method again.

1. Factorial (n!)

factorial(n) = n * factorial(n - 1), with factorial(0) = 1 as the base case.

2. Fibonacci Sequence

fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2), with fib(0) = 0 and fib(1) = 1 as base cases.

3. Sum of an Array

Recursively add the first element to the sum of the rest of the array.

expert.content:
Visualizing the Recursion Tree - factorial(4)

factorial(4)
  = 4 * factorial(3)
        = 3 * factorial(2)
              = 2 * factorial(1)
                    = 1 * factorial(0)
                          = 1              <-- base case hit
                    = 1 * 1 = 1
              = 2 * 1 = 2
        = 3 * 2 = 6
  = 4 * 6 = 24
Each call waits on the stack for the call below it to return - this is why deep recursion consumes stack memory proportional to the recursion depth, O(n) for factorial(n).

Why Naive Fibonacci Recursion Is Expensive

fib(n) as written above recomputes the same sub-values repeatedly - fib(2) is computed multiple times inside fib(5), for example. This gives an exponential O(2^n) time complexity. 
                      fib(5)
                    /        \
               fib(4)          fib(3)
              /      \        /      \
         fib(3)     fib(2)  fib(2)   fib(1)
         /    \      /  \    /  \
     fib(2) fib(1) fib(1)fib(0)fib(1)fib(0)
     /  \
  fib(1)fib(0)

Notice fib(3), fib(2), fib(1) are each recomputed multiple times - wasted work.

Stack Depth and StackOverflowError

Every recursive call pushes a new stack frame. If the base case is never reached (or recursion is too deep for the input), the JVM throws a StackOverflowError. This is the #1 real-world bug in recursive code.

Tail Recursion (and Java's Lack of Tail-Call Optimization)

A tail-recursive method's recursive call is the very last operation - no pending work remains after it returns. Some languages optimize this into a loop internally, but the JVM does not perform tail-call optimization, so even a tail-recursive Java method still consumes O(n) stack frames.

Recursion vs Iteration

AspectRecursionIteration
Readability for divide-and-conquer problemsOften clearerCan get complex
Memory usageO(depth) stack framesO(1) typically
RiskStackOverflowError on deep recursionNone from depth
PerformanceFunction-call overhead per stepUsually faster

What are the two required parts of any recursive method?A base case and a recursive case that moves toward the base case
What is the time complexity of naive recursive Fibonacci?O(2^n) - exponential, due to repeated recomputation of the same sub-problems
What causes a StackOverflowError?Recursion that never reaches its base case, or recursion deeper than the JVM's stack size allows
Does Java optimize tail recursion into a loop?No - unlike some functional languages, the JVM does not perform tail-call optimization
What is the space complexity of a recursive call with depth n?O(n), one stack frame per active call
How can you convert naive recursive Fibonacci to run efficiently?Use memoization (top-down) or tabulation (bottom-up) - see the Dynamic Programming topic
When would you prefer recursion over a loop?When the problem is naturally self-similar (tree traversal, divide and conquer, backtracking) and depth is bounded

beginner.content:
Backtracking is a technique for solving problems by trying out possible options one at a time, and undoing (backtracking) a choice as soon as it is discovered to be wrong, then trying the next option.

Think of it as exploring a maze: you walk forward, and if you hit a dead end, you step back to the last junction and try a different path - instead of restarting from scratch.

It is commonly used for:
• Generating all subsets/permutations
• The N-Queens puzzle
• Sudoku solvers
• Maze solving

1. Generating All Subsets of a Set

For each element, we make two choices: include it, or don't. Backtracking explores both branches and undoes the choice after exploring it.

2. The Core Backtracking Pattern

Every backtracking solution follows this shape:

1. Choose - make a choice (add to current path).
2. Explore - recurse with that choice in place.
3. Un-choose (backtrack) - remove the choice before trying the next option.

This "choose, explore, un-choose" pattern is exactly what you saw with current.add(...) and current.remove(...) in the subsets example above.

expert.content:
The N-Queens Problem

Place N queens on an N x N chessboard so that no two queens attack each other (no shared row, column, or diagonal). Backtracking places queens column by column, and backtracks whenever a placement is unsafe.

Visualizing the Backtracking Search Tree (N=4, first 2 columns)

col=0: try row 0 -----> col=1: row 0 UNSAFE (same row)
                                       row 1 UNSAFE (diagonal)
                                       row 2 SAFE -> continue to col=2 ...
                                       row 3 SAFE -> continue to col=2 ...

col=0: try row 1 -----> col=1: row 0 UNSAFE (diagonal)
                                       ... (backtrack further down)

Whenever no row is safe at a column, we backtrack to the previous
column and try its next candidate row.
Printing One N-Queens Solution as a Board

Backtracking Complexity

Backtracking is fundamentally exhaustive search with early pruning - it explores a decision tree but cuts off (prunes) branches that cannot lead to a valid solution, which is far better than brute force but still exponential in the worst case.

ProblemNaive Brute ForceWith Backtracking Pruning
N-QueensO(N^N)Much smaller in practice due to isSafe() pruning
Subsets of n elementsO(2^n)O(2^n) (all subsets are valid, no pruning possible)
Sudoku (9x9)9^81 (astronomical)Feasible in milliseconds with constraint pruning

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is backtracking?A systematic trial-and-undo search technique that explores choices and abandons ("backtracks" from) any that cannot lead to a valid solution
How is backtracking different from plain recursion?Backtracking explicitly undoes a choice (state change) after exploring it, so the same shared state can be reused for the next branch
What is "pruning" in backtracking?Skipping branches early once you know they cannot possibly succeed (e.g., isSafe() check in N-Queens)
Name three classic backtracking problems.N-Queens, Sudoku solver, subset/permutation generation, maze/path-finding
What is the time complexity of generating all subsets of n elements?O(2^n) - every element is either included or excluded
Why does the N-Queens solution overwrite board[col] instead of removing it explicitly?Because the array slot is simply reassigned in the next loop iteration - that reassignment itself acts as the "un-choose" step
Is backtracking the same as Dynamic Programming?No - DP reuses overlapping sub-problem results, while backtracking explores and discards paths without memoizing results

beginner.content:
A Greedy Algorithm builds up a solution piece by piece, always choosing the option that looks best right now (locally optimal), hoping this leads to the overall best (globally optimal) solution.

Greedy algorithms are simple and fast, but they do not always produce the correct/optimal answer - that only happens when the problem has a special structure ("greedy choice property").

Classic examples: Coin Change (with standard currency), Activity Selection, and Minimum Spanning Tree algorithms like Prim's/Kruskal's.

1. Coin Change (Greedy Version)

Given coin denominations, find the minimum number of coins to make a target amount by always picking the largest coin that fits.

2. Activity Selection Problem

Given start/end times of activities, select the maximum number of non-overlapping activities. The greedy strategy: always pick the activity that finishes earliest among the remaining valid options.

expert.content:
When Greedy Fails: Coin Change With a Non-Standard Set

The greedy "pick largest coin first" strategy only works for well-behaved (canonical) coin systems like {1, 5, 10, 25}. With arbitrary denominations, greedy can give a wrong (non-optimal) answer.

Fractional Knapsack (Greedy Works Here)

Unlike 0/1 Knapsack (which needs Dynamic Programming), the Fractional Knapsack allows taking a fraction of an item, and here the greedy strategy - always take the item with highest value/weight ratio first - is provably optimal.

Greedy vs Dynamic Programming

AspectGreedyDynamic Programming
Decision makingLocally optimal choice, never revisitedExplores/combines all sub-problem results
Guarantees global optimum?Only for problems with the greedy-choice propertyYes, if the recurrence and base cases are correct
SpeedUsually faster, O(n log n) or O(n)Usually slower, O(n²) or more
Example where each winsActivity Selection, Fractional Knapsack0/1 Knapsack, Coin Change (general denominations)

How to Recognize a Greedy-Friendly Problem

A problem is safe for a greedy approach only if it has both:
• Greedy choice property - a locally optimal choice leads toward a globally optimal solution.
• Optimal substructure - an optimal solution to the problem contains optimal solutions to its sub-problems.

If you cannot prove the greedy choice property holds, do not trust a greedy solution - verify it against brute force on small inputs, or use Dynamic Programming instead.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is a Greedy Algorithm?An algorithm that makes the locally optimal choice at each step, hoping it leads to a global optimum
Does greedy always give the optimal solution?No - only for problems having the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure
Give an example where greedy Coin Change fails.Denominations {1, 3, 4} for amount 6 - greedy gives [4,1,1] (3 coins) instead of the optimal [3,3] (2 coins)
Is Fractional Knapsack solvable by greedy?Yes - sorting by value/weight ratio and taking greedily is provably optimal
Is 0/1 Knapsack solvable by greedy?No - it requires Dynamic Programming since items cannot be split
What is the time complexity of the Activity Selection greedy algorithm?O(n log n), dominated by sorting activities by finish time
Name two more classic greedy algorithms.Kruskal's/Prim's Minimum Spanning Tree, Dijkstra's Shortest Path, Huffman Coding

beginner.content:
Dynamic Programming (DP) is a technique for solving problems by breaking them into overlapping sub-problems, solving each sub-problem only once, and reusing (caching) the result the next time it's needed.

DP applies when a problem has:
• Overlapping sub-problems - the same smaller problem is solved again and again.
• Optimal substructure - the overall solution can be built from optimal solutions to sub-problems.

There are two ways to implement DP:
• Memoization (top-down) - recursion + a cache.
• Tabulation (bottom-up) - an iterative table built from the smallest sub-problem upward.

1. Naive Recursive Fibonacci (No DP)

This is correct but slow - it recomputes the same values repeatedly.

2. Fibonacci With Memoization (Top-Down DP)

Store each computed result in a cache array so it is never recomputed.

3. Fibonacci With Tabulation (Bottom-Up DP)

Build the answer iteratively from the smallest sub-problems up, avoiding recursion entirely.

expert.content:
Performance Comparison: Naive vs Memoized vs Tabulated

Run all three approaches for fib(40) and compare - naive recursion becomes noticeably slow while the DP versions stay instant.

Complexity Comparison

ApproachTime ComplexitySpace ComplexityNotes
Naive RecursionO(2^n)O(n) stackExponential - unusable beyond n ~ 40
Memoization (top-down)O(n)O(n) cache + O(n) stackEasy to derive from naive recursion
Tabulation (bottom-up)O(n)O(n) tableNo recursion, no stack overflow risk
Tabulation (space-optimized)O(n)O(1)Only keep last 2 values, not the full table

Space-Optimized Tabulation

Since Fibonacci only ever needs the previous two values, we can drop the array entirely and use two variables - O(1) space instead of O(n).

Another Classic: 0/1 Knapsack With DP

Given item weights/values and a capacity, choose a subset maximizing value without exceeding capacity - each item is either fully taken or not (unlike Fractional Knapsack, greedy does NOT work here).

Recognizing DP Problems

Does the problem ask you to find a MIN / MAX / COUNT
of ways, given choices at each step?
        |
        v
Can the problem be broken into smaller sub-problems
that overlap (the same sub-problem recurs)?
        |
        v
   YES to both  --> candidate for Dynamic Programming
   NO           --> plain recursion, greedy, or divide & conquer instead

Interview Questions

What two properties must a problem have for DP to apply?Overlapping sub-problems and optimal substructure
What is the difference between memoization and tabulation?Memoization is top-down recursion with caching; tabulation is bottom-up iteration filling a table
What is the time complexity of naive recursive Fibonacci?O(2^n) - exponential due to repeated recomputation
What is the time complexity of memoized/tabulated Fibonacci?O(n) - each sub-problem computed exactly once
How can you reduce Fibonacci DP space from O(n) to O(1)?Only keep the last two computed values in variables instead of a full array
Why doesn't Greedy work for 0/1 Knapsack?Local best-ratio choices can block a better combination since items can't be split - it lacks the greedy-choice property
What data structure is typically used in tabulated DP for 2D problems?A 2D array/table, e.g. dp[i][w] for Knapsack, indexed by item count and remaining capacity
What is the risk of memoization for very large n?Deep recursion can cause a StackOverflowError even though results are cached - tabulation avoids this

beginner.content:
Divide and Conquer is a strategy for solving a problem by breaking it into three steps:

• Divide - split the problem into smaller sub-problems of the same type.
• Conquer - solve each sub-problem recursively (small enough sub-problems are solved directly).
• Combine - merge the sub-problem results into the final solution.

Classic examples: Merge Sort, Quick Sort, and Binary Search all use this pattern.

1. Binary Search: The Simplest Divide and Conquer

Binary Search divides the array in half each time, conquers by checking the middle, and there's nothing to combine since only one half is ever explored.

2. Merge Sort: Divide, Conquer, and Combine

Merge Sort demonstrates all three steps clearly: divide the array in half, conquer by recursively sorting each half, then combine by merging the two sorted halves.

expert.content:
Visualizing the Divide / Conquer / Combine Pattern

                     ORIGINAL PROBLEM
                            |
                        DIVIDE
                            |
              +-------------+-------------+
              |                           |
        SUB-PROBLEM 1               SUB-PROBLEM 2
              |                           |
          (recurse:                  (recurse:
        divide again until               divide again until
         base case)                       base case)
              |                           |
          CONQUER                     CONQUER
        (solved directly              (solved directly
         at base case)                 at base case)
              |                           |
              +-------------+-------------+
                            |
                        COMBINE
                            |
                     FINAL SOLUTION

Finding Max and Min With Divide and Conquer

Instead of a simple linear scan, we can split the array, find max/min of each half recursively, then combine by comparing the two pairs - useful for illustrating combine logic beyond sorting/searching.

Analyzing Complexity With the Master Theorem

Divide and conquer recurrences typically look like T(n) = a*T(n/b) + f(n), where the problem of size n is split into a sub-problems of size n/b, plus f(n) work to combine.

AlgorithmRecurrenceResulting Complexity
Binary SearchT(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)O(log n)
Merge SortT(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)O(n log n)
Quick Sort (avg case)T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)O(n log n)
Naive Matrix Multiply (D&C)T(n) = 8T(n/2) + O(n²)O(n³)

Divide and Conquer vs Dynamic Programming

AspectDivide and ConquerDynamic Programming
Sub-problemsIndependent, non-overlappingOverlapping - same sub-problem reused
Caching needed?NoYes - memoization/tabulation
Typical examplesMerge Sort, Quick Sort, Binary SearchFibonacci (DP version), Knapsack, LCS

If sub-problems overlap, plain divide and conquer wastes time recomputing them - that is exactly the signal to switch to Dynamic Programming instead.

beginner.content:
A graph is a collection of nodes (vertices) connected by edges. Graphs model networks: social connections, road maps, web pages, and more.

The most common way to represent a graph in code is an adjacency list - for each node, keep a list of the nodes it directly connects to.

The two fundamental ways to explore (traverse) a graph are:
• BFS (Breadth-First Search) - explore level by level, using a Queue.
• DFS (Depth-First Search) - explore as deep as possible before backtracking, using a Stack (or recursion).
1. Representing a Graph With an Adjacency List

2. Breadth-First Search (BFS)

BFS starts at a node, visits all its direct neighbors first, then their neighbors, and so on - using a Queue to track what to visit next.

3. Depth-First Search (DFS)

DFS goes as deep as possible down one path before backtracking - naturally expressed with recursion.

expert.content:
Iterative DFS (Using an Explicit Stack)

DFS is usually written recursively, but it can also be done iteratively with your own Stack, which avoids recursion-depth limits on very deep/large graphs.

BFS for Shortest Path (Unweighted Graph)

Because BFS explores level by level, the first time it reaches a node is guaranteed to be via the shortest path (fewest edges) in an unweighted graph.

Visualizing BFS vs DFS Traversal Order

Graph:
        0
       / \
      1   2
     / \   \
    3   4---+

BFS from 0 (level by level, Queue):
  Level 0: 0
  Level 1: 1, 2
  Level 2: 3, 4
  Order: 0 1 2 3 4

DFS from 0 (go deep first, Stack/recursion):
  0 -> 1 -> 3 (dead end, backtrack)
       1 -> 4 -> 2 (already reachable, backtrack)
  Order: 0 1 3 4 2

BFS vs DFS Comparison

AspectBFSDFS
Data structureQueueStack (or recursion)
Time ComplexityO(V + E)O(V + E)
Space ComplexityO(V)O(V)
Shortest path (unweighted)?YesNo
Good forShortest path, level-order problemsCycle detection, topological sort, path existence, maze solving
V = number of vertices, E = number of edges.

What data structure does BFS use, and why?A Queue (FIFO) - ensures nodes are visited in the order they were discovered, i.e. level by level
What data structure does DFS use, and why?A Stack (LIFO) or recursion - naturally explores as deep as possible before backtracking
What is the time complexity of both BFS and DFS?O(V + E), visiting every vertex and edge once
Why does BFS find the shortest path in an unweighted graph?It explores nodes strictly in increasing order of distance from the source, so the first visit is always via the shortest path

beginner.content:
A tree is a hierarchical data structure made of nodes, where each node has a value and links to child nodes. A Binary Tree restricts each node to at most two children - "left" and "right".

Traversal means visiting every node exactly once in some defined order. The three classic Depth-First traversal orders for binary trees are:
• Inorder (Left, Root, Right)
• Preorder (Root, Left, Right)
• Postorder (Left, Right, Root)
1. Defining a Binary Tree Node

2. Inorder Traversal (Left, Root, Right)

For a Binary Search Tree, inorder traversal visits nodes in ascending sorted order.

3. Preorder Traversal (Root, Left, Right)

Useful for creating a copy of the tree, or serializing its structure.

4. Postorder Traversal (Left, Right, Root)

Useful for safely deleting a tree (children before parent) or evaluating expression trees.

expert.content:
Level Order Traversal (Breadth-First, Using a Queue)

Unlike the three DFS-style traversals above, Level Order visits nodes level by level using a Queue - the tree equivalent of Graph BFS.

Visualizing All Traversal Orders on One Tree

          4
        /   \
       2     6
      / \   / \
     1   3 5   7

Inorder   (L,Root,R): 1 2 3 4 5 6 7   <- sorted order for a BST
Preorder  (Root,L,R): 4 2 1 3 6 5 7   <- good for cloning/serializing
Postorder (L,R,Root): 1 3 2 5 7 6 4   <- good for safe deletion
Level Order (BFS):    4 2 6 1 3 5 7   <- good for level-by-level processing

Computing Height (Max Depth) of a Binary Tree

A recursive tree algorithm: height of a node = 1 + max(height of left subtree, height of right subtree).

Iterative Inorder Traversal (Using an Explicit Stack)

Recursive traversal is elegant but uses the call stack implicitly; production code sometimes needs an iterative version to avoid deep-recursion stack overflow on very unbalanced trees.

Traversal Complexity Comparison

TraversalOrderTimeSpaceCommon Use
InorderLeft, Root, RightO(n)O(h)Sorted output of a BST
PreorderRoot, Left, RightO(n)O(h)Cloning / serializing a tree
PostorderLeft, Right, RootO(n)O(h)Deleting a tree, expression evaluation

n = number of nodes, h = height of the tree (recursion/stack depth).

Interview Questions

What is the order of an inorder traversal?Left subtree, then Root, then Right subtree
Why does inorder traversal of a BST give sorted output?Because in a BST, every left subtree holds smaller values and every right subtree holds larger values than the root, and inorder visits left-root-right accordingly
Which traversal is best for safely deleting a tree?Postorder - children are deleted before their parent
Which traversal is best for cloning/serializing a tree?Preorder - root is recorded before its children, matching reconstruction order

What is Big-O Notation?

Big-O notation describes how the running time (or memory usage) of a program grows as the input size (usually called n) grows.

It answers one question: "If I double my input, roughly how much slower does my code get?"

• Big-O describes the worst case / upper bound — the maximum amount of work the algorithm could possibly do for a given input size.
• It ignores machine speed, JVM warm-up, constant factors — it only cares about the shape of growth as n gets large.
• It is written as O(f(n)), e.g. O(n), O(n^2), O(log n).

Think of Big-O as a "speed label" on an algorithm, similar to how a car has a fuel-efficiency rating — it tells you what to expect, not the exact number for every trip.

O(1) — Constant Time

The operation takes the same amount of time no matter how big the input is. Accessing an array element by index is the classic example — the JVM computes the memory address directly, it does not scan anything.

O(n) — Linear Time

The work grows directly proportional to the input size. A single loop over every element of an array/list is the textbook example — double the elements, double the time.

O(n^2) — Quadratic Time

Occurs with nested loops where each loop runs roughly n times — total work is n * n. This is common in naive algorithms like Bubble Sort or brute-force pair comparisons.

O(log n) — Logarithmic Time

The problem size is cut in half (or divided) each step, so the work grows very slowly even for huge inputs. Binary search on a sorted array is the classic example — searching 1,000,000 elements takes only about 20 comparisons, not 1,000,000.

intermediate.content:
Deriving Big-O from Code — A Practical Method

When looking at a method, ask:

1. Single loop over n items? → O(n)
2. Loop nested inside another loop, both over n? → O(n^2)
3. Loop that divides the problem in half each time (like binary search)? → O(log n)
4. Loop over n combined with a divide-and-conquer sort/recursion (like Merge Sort)? → O(n log n)
5. Recursion that branches into 2 calls per level (like naive Fibonacci)? → O(2^n)

Rule of thumb: count the loops that depend on n, multiply their bounds together, then drop constants and lower-order terms — see the Expert section for a full worked example.

Why is ArrayList.get() O(1) but LinkedList.get() O(n)? ArrayList is backed by a real array in memory, so index access is a direct memory offset calculation. LinkedList is a chain of nodes with pointers — to reach index 500 it must walk 500 node links from the head (or tail, whichever is closer).

Common Mistakes When Analyzing Complexity

• Forgetting hidden loops inside library calls: list.contains(x) on an ArrayList is O(n) internally - calling it inside another loop silently creates O(n^2).

• Mixing up best case and worst case: Big-O is the worst case / upper bound; the best case is described by Big-Omega, and when both match, by Big-Theta.
• Assuming string concatenation is O(1): str += x in a loop is O(n) per concatenation because Strings are immutable, making the whole loop O(n^2) - use StringBuilder instead.

What is Big-Omega (Ω)?

Big-Omega notation describes the lower bound / best case of an algorithm — the minimum amount of work it will ever do for a given input size n.

Where Big-O (O) asks "how bad can it get?", Big-Omega (Ω) asks "how good can it get?"

• Written as Ω(f(n)), e.g. Ω(1), Ω(n).
• It represents the fastest the algorithm could possibly finish, under the luckiest possible input.
• It does NOT mean "average case" — it is strictly the best-case floor.

Ω(1) — Best Case is Instant

Linear Search over an array is O(n) in the worst case (the target is missing or at the very end), but its best case is Ω(1) — the target happens to be the very first element checked.

Ω(n) — When Best Case Still Requires a Full Pass

Some algorithms have no "lucky shortcut" — every single input forces at least n units of work, even in the best case. Summing all elements of an array is a simple example: there is no early exit, so the best case and worst case are the same order of growth.

Why Big-Omega Matters

Big-Omega is useful when you want to know the guaranteed minimum cost of an operation — for example, proving that no comparison-based sorting algorithm can do better than Ω(n log n) in the worst case across all inputs (a famous theoretical lower bound), or showing that even the luckiest run of your algorithm cannot be faster than a certain threshold.

For Linear Search: worst case O(n), best case Ω(1) - since O and Ω differ, Linear Search has no single Θ that covers all inputs generally (though for the "target always missing" family of inputs it is Θ(n)).

expert.content:
Formal Definition

f(n) = Ω(g(n)) means there exist positive constants c and n0 such that f(n) >= c * g(n) for all n >= n0. In plain terms: beyond some point, the algorithm's running time never dips below a constant multiple of g(n).

Common Mistakes

• Treating Ω as "average case": Ω is strictly the best case, not the typical/average case - average case needs separate probabilistic analysis.
• Assuming every algorithm has a meaningful Ω that differs from its O: for algorithms like array traversal that always do exactly n work, Ω(n) equals O(n), so it's simply Θ(n).
• Forgetting Ω is per-algorithm, not per-problem, unless stated as a theoretical bound: "sorting is Ω(n log n)" refers to the best any comparison-based algorithm CAN do, not any single algorithm's best case.

beginner.content:
What is Big-Theta (Θ)?

Big-Theta notation describes a tight bound — it applies when the best case and worst case grow at the same rate. In that situation, Big-O (upper bound) and Big-Omega (lower bound) meet, and Theta gives the single, precise growth rate.

• Written as Θ(f(n)).
• If an algorithm is Θ(n), it means it ALWAYS does work proportional to n — never faster, never slower, regardless of the specific input.
• Theta is the most informative notation when it applies, because it pins down behavior exactly instead of just bounding it from one side.

Θ(n) — Simple Single-Pass Sum

Summing every element of an array always visits every element exactly once — there is no lucky shortcut and no unlucky slowdown. Best case = worst case = Θ(n).

Θ(1) — Array Index Access

Accessing arr[i] always costs the same, single operation, for any array, any index, any input. Best case and worst case are identical, so it is Θ(1).

When Theta Does NOT Apply

Linear Search does not have a single overall Theta, because its best case (target found first, Ω(1)) and worst case (target missing, O(n)) grow at different rates. Theta only applies when those two bounds match.

Merge Sort is a great example: unlike Quick Sort (which degrades to O(n^2) on bad pivots) or Bubble Sort without early-exit optimization, Merge Sort always splits and merges in the same pattern regardless of input order, so its best and worst case coincide at Θ(n log n).

beginner.content:
What is Time Complexity?

Time complexity measures how the number of operations an algorithm performs grows as the input size n grows. It is not measured in seconds (that depends on the CPU, JVM warm-up, and system load) — instead it counts basic operations: comparisons, assignments, arithmetic, and array/collection accesses.

We express time complexity using Big-O, Big-Omega, or Big-Theta notation depending on which bound we care about.

Counting Operations — A Simple Example

To find time complexity, literally count how many times each line executes as a function of n.

Dropping Constants

Two separate loops, each running n times, is n + n = 2n operations — but Big-O drops the constant multiplier 2, because it does not change the growth SHAPE, only the steepness.

Dropping Lower-Order Terms

If a method does O(n^2) work AND O(n) work, the O(n) part becomes irrelevant as n grows huge — so we only keep the fastest-growing (dominant) term.

Time Complexity of Recursive Calls

For recursive methods, count how many times the method is called, multiplied by the work done per call. A recursive method that halves its input each call and does O(1) work per call, like binary search, is O(log n). A recursive method that spawns 2 calls per level, like naive Fibonacci, is O(2^n).

beginner.content:
What is Space Complexity?

Space complexity measures how much extra memory an algorithm needs, relative to the input size n. Just like time complexity, we express it using Big-O notation — O(1), O(n), O(n^2), etc.

Total memory usage has two parts:
• Input space — the memory taken by the input itself (usually not counted).
• Auxiliary space — the EXTRA memory the algorithm allocates while running (this is what "space complexity" almost always refers to).

When people say "this algorithm is O(n) space", they mean it uses auxiliary space proportional to n, beyond the input it was given.

O(1) Space — No Extra Memory Needed

An algorithm that only uses a fixed number of variables, regardless of input size, has constant space complexity.

O(n) Space — Extra Memory Proportional to Input

If an algorithm creates a new array/list/map whose size grows with the input, its space complexity is O(n).

Auxiliary Space vs Total Space

Given an input array of size n, if a method just reads it without allocating anything new, the auxiliary space is O(1), even though the total space (input + auxiliary) is O(n). Interviewers almost always mean auxiliary space when they ask "what's the space complexity?"

intermediate.content:
Recursion Uses Stack Space Too

Every recursive call adds a new frame to the JVM's call stack, holding local variables and the return address. A recursive function that goes n levels deep uses O(n) auxiliary space for that stack — even if it allocates no arrays or objects at all. The iterative equivalent, using a simple loop, uses O(1) space instead.

Deep Recursion Can Overflow the Stack

Because each recursive call consumes real stack memory, a recursive method with O(n) call-stack depth on a very large n can throw StackOverflowError - something an O(1)-space iterative loop never risks, since it doesn't grow the call stack at all.

Time-Space Tradeoffs

Algorithms often trade memory for speed. A classic example: recursive Fibonacci without memoization is O(2^n) time but only O(n) space (call stack depth). Adding a memoization cache (HashMap) increases space to O(n) - wait, actually reduces time to O(n) at the cost of O(n) space for the cache, on top of the O(n) recursion stack.

• Forgetting recursion has hidden stack cost - a "space O(1)" recursive method is a myth; every level of recursion adds a stack frame.
• Counting input space as auxiliary space - if a method just reads its input array without copying it, that array does not count toward auxiliary space.
• Ignoring space used by return values - a method that builds and returns a new O(n) list should be counted as O(n) space, not O(1), even though "no local variables" might look small.
• Assuming in-place algorithms are always O(1) space - "in-place" refers to not needing a full copy of the input, but some in-place algorithms still use O(log n) recursion stack space (e.g. in-place Quick Sort).

beginner.content:
What is Amortized Complexity?

Amortized complexity describes the average cost per operation over a long sequence of operations, even when a few individual operations in that sequence are much more expensive than the rest.

It is NOT the same as "average case" (which is about typical input). Amortized analysis is about spreading out the cost of occasional expensive operations across many cheap ones, so the per-operation cost, averaged over the whole sequence, stays low.

The textbook Java example is ArrayList.add() — most calls are O(1), but every so often the internal array is full and must be resized, which is O(n). Yet across n total additions, the AVERAGE cost per add is still O(1) — this is called amortized O(1).

Why ArrayList.add() Is Usually O(1)

An ArrayList is backed by a fixed-size array. As long as there's room, adding an element just places it in the next free slot — that's O(1).

The Occasional Expensive Resize

When the backing array is full, ArrayList must allocate a NEW, larger array and copy every existing element into it — an O(n) operation — before the new element can be added.

intermediate.content:
Averaging the Cost Across n Additions

Suppose we add n elements one at a time, and the array doubles in size every time it fills up (a common growth strategy). The resize costs happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ... — a geometric sequence.

Total cost of all resizes combined: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + ... + n ≈ 2n (a geometric series sums to roughly twice the final size).

Total cost of all n insertions (cheap O(1) ones) plus all resize copying = n + 2n = 3n.

Average cost per operation = 3n / n = 3 = a constant, independent of n. That constant-per-operation average is exactly what "amortized O(1)" means.

The Doubling Strategy Visualized

Capacity growth: 1 -> 2 -> 4 -> 8 -> 16 -> 32 ...

add() calls:  1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8   9  ...
Cost:         1   R2  1   R4  1   1   1   R8  1  ...
              ^   ^       ^               ^
              |   |       |               |
           cheap resize cheap          resize
           O(1)  O(n)  O(1)             O(n)

Even though resizes (R) cost O(n), they get RARER as capacity grows -
they happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32... (doubling), so their total
combined cost across n adds is only about 2n, not n^2.

Spread that 2n resize cost evenly across all n add() calls:
  amortized cost per add = O(1)
This is why doubling (rather than, say, growing by a fixed +1 each time) is essential — growing by a constant amount instead of a multiplicative factor would make total resize cost O(n^2), NOT amortized O(1).

Amortized vs Worst-Case vs Average-Case

TermMeaning
Worst-case (Big-O)Cost of the single most expensive operation, considered in isolation
Average-caseExpected cost assuming some probability distribution over inputs
AmortizedTotal cost of a SEQUENCE of n operations, divided by n - guaranteed even for adversarial inputs, unlike average-case

Amortized O(1) for ArrayList.add() means: any single call could be O(n) in the worst case (during a resize), but no matter what sequence of adds you perform, the TOTAL cost of n adds is never worse than O(n) - guaranteed, not probabilistic.

Amortized Analysis via the "Accounting Method" (Banker's Method)

One common way to formally prove amortized O(1): imagine each add() call is "charged" a constant number of extra credits (say, 3 units) even though it only needs 1 unit for the cheap case. The unused credits from cheap operations are saved up and used to "pay" for the expensive resize when it happens - so no operation ever appears to exceed its flat charged cost when viewed over the whole sequence.

Common Mistakes When Reasoning About Amortized Complexity

• Confusing amortized O(1) with worst-case O(1) - a single ArrayList.add() call CAN still be O(n) if it happens to trigger a resize; amortized only guarantees the average over many calls. In latency-sensitive real-time code, this occasional spike can matter.
• Assuming any growable structure has amortized O(1) growth - it depends entirely on the growth strategy. Growing capacity by a FIXED amount (e.g. +1 or +10 each time) instead of a multiplicative factor makes total resize cost O(n^2), destroying the amortized O(1) guarantee.
• Forgetting HashMap resizing follows the same idea - put() is amortized O(1) average because the bucket array also doubles when the load factor threshold is crossed.
• Treating amortized cost as a per-call promise - it is a promise about the SEQUENCE total, not any individual call.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is amortized complexity?The average cost per operation across a long sequence, even when some individual operations are expensive
Why is ArrayList.add() called "amortized O(1)"?Most calls are O(1); occasional O(n) resizes are rare enough (due to capacity doubling) that their total cost averages out to O(1) per call
Is amortized the same as average-case?No - amortized is a guaranteed bound over any sequence of operations; average-case depends on input probability distribution
Can a single ArrayList.add() call still be O(n)?Yes - if it triggers a resize; amortized O(1) is about the sequence total, not any one call
Why does doubling capacity give amortized O(1), but growing by +1 each time does not?Doubling makes resizes exponentially rarer, keeping total resize cost at O(n); fixed-increment growth causes O(n) resizes on nearly every add, giving O(n^2) total
What is the accounting/banker's method?A proof technique that charges each cheap operation a slightly higher flat cost, banking the surplus credits to pay for future expensive operations
Name another Java operation with amortized O(1) cost.StringBuilder.append() and HashMap.put() - both use similar doubling/resizing strategies
Does amortized analysis assume random/average input?No - it holds even for the worst possible sequence of operations, which is what makes it a strong guarantee

Big-Omega - Lower bound (best case) growth rate of an algorithm
Big-Theta - Tight bound, used when best case and worst case match
O(1) - Constant time, e.g. array index access
O(log n) - Logarithmic time, e.g. binary search
O(n) - Linear time, e.g. a single loop over an array
O(n log n) - Linearithmic time, e.g. merge sort, quick sort average case
O(n^2) - Quadratic time, e.g. bubble sort, nested loops

Recursion - A function calling itself with a base case to stop
Backtracking - Recursive search that undoes ("backtracks") choices that fail
Dynamic Programming - Solving overlapping subproblems once and caching results
Greedy Algorithm - Makes the locally optimal choice at each step, not always globally optimal
Divide and Conquer - Break a problem into subproblems, solve, then combine
BFS - Breadth-First Search, explores a graph level by level using a queue
DFS - Depth-First Search, explores a graph as deep as possible before backtracking
